props.title: Scream
props.initialSlug: Small town killer terrorizes teens with horror trivia

sections.content: Scream (1996) revolutionized horror by turning the genre's tropes inside out. Wes Craven's masterpiece follows Sidney Prescott as she faces off against Ghostface while the film simultaneously deconstructs slasher conventions. The brilliant opening sequence with Drew Barrymore established that no character was safe, while Randy's "rules of horror" speech explicitly laid out the clichés the film would both mock and embrace. This self-awareness influenced countless films like I Know What You Did Last Summer (1997) and Urban Legend (1998), launching a wave of meta-horror that continues with movies like The Cabin in the Woods (2012).

sections.content: The film's success sparked a renaissance in teen horror. The Faculty (1998) mixed Scream's self-referential style with sci-fi paranoia. Cherry Falls (2000) inverted the virgin-survives trope. Final Destination (2000) kept the knowing teens but replaced the human killer with Death itself. The meta approach peaked with Behind the Mask: The Rise of Leslie Vernon (2006), which treated slasher killers as athletes training for their big night.

Scream's influence extends beyond horror. Its pop culture-savvy characters and blend of comedy with scares influenced dialogue-heavy teen films like Cruel Intentions (1999) and Mean Girls (2004). The film's success also revived Wes Craven's career, leading to Red Eye (2005) and future Scream sequels that continued examining how horror evolves with technology and social media. sections.content: The iconic Ghostface mask, inspired by Edvard Munch's "The Scream," became instantly recognizable horror imagery alongside Michael Myers and Jason Voorhees. The killer's methodology - using horror knowledge as a weapon through trivia phone calls - created a template copied in films like Scary Movie (2000) and Cherry Falls (2000). The whodunit element strengthened by having multiple killers became a franchise staple, influencing neo-slashers like You're Next (2011).
